post.title: What systematic disagreement reveals that consensus never will
post.content:
If you run an annotation project and your inter-annotator agreement score comes back low, the reflex is to retrain annotators, clarify guidelines, or impose a majority vote. This is not wrong. But it treats disagreement as a problem to be solved, and sometimes disagreement is a measurement you should be reading.

Label disagreement — the phenomenon where two or more trained annotators consistently assign different labels to the same items — is widely documented in ML literature. It shows up in sentiment analysis, medical imaging, legal document classification, content moderation. And in almost every case, the institutional response is the same: adjudicate toward consensus, update the guideline, move on. What almost nobody does is treat the disagreement itself as data.

Here is what I keep seeing when teams actually audit their disagreement patterns.

The items annotators fight over are not random. Disagreement is not evenly distributed across a dataset. It clusters. A team annotating customer support tickets for urgency will find that annotators disagree strongly on a specific subset — say, tickets that mention a deadline but do not state a consequence. These items are not harder to annotate because annotators are careless. They are harder because the category boundary is genuinely ambiguous in those cases, and the ambiguity lives in the definition of the category, not in the annotators.

A second example from a different domain: teams annotating news articles for harmful content or misinformation almost always find disagreement spikes around satire, opinion pieces that use strong language, and articles that quote harmful claims without endorsing them. The annotators are not confused — they are applying different implicit theories of what endorsement means. The disagreement tells you that your category definition includes a contested philosophical question, and no amount of guideline retraining resolves it unless you surface and decide that question explicitly.

When you suppress disagreement via adjudication — where a senior reviewer picks the right answer and the item becomes consensus — you remove the signal. The dataset now contains a silent editorial decision: someone decided this ticket is urgent. But the decision was made once, by one person, and the reasoning was never surfaced. The dataset does not remember that this was a close call.

This matters for a specific reason: models trained on adjudicated labels learn the adjudicators’ intuitions, not the true structure of the category. If your senior reviewer has a bias — toward flagging urgency when deadlines are present, regardless of consequence — the model will learn that bias. And you will not find it by looking at accuracy numbers. You will find it by going back to the disagreement log and asking: where did we disagree, and what did the person who overrode us actually decide?

A useful thought experiment. Take your held-out test set. For every item where annotators originally disagreed, set aside the final label and replace it with the adjudicated one. Now train two models: one on the original labels with disagreement intact, perhaps labeled as uncertain, one on the adjudicated labels. Compare their error profiles. I do not have systematic data across many projects, but I have seen enough single-project comparisons to believe the disagreement-supervised model typically surfaces different errors — specifically, errors on the items the team originally argued about. Those errors are a more honest picture of where the category boundary is unclear.

The practical implication is not that you should never adjudicate. It is that adjudication should be documented and the disagreement log should be treated as a first-class artifact. The items where annotators fought the longest are the items that most need to be revisited, not because the dataset is broken, but because those are exactly the items where the model’s behavior on them will be most sensitive to how you decided to resolve the dispute.

There is a second-order effect worth noting. When teams suppress disagreement consistently — always adjudicating toward consensus, never surfacing the close calls — they end up with a dataset that looks cleaner than it is. The model’s training data contains no record of the genuine ambiguity in the domain. This creates a calibration problem: the model will express high confidence on items that happen to land in clear consensus territory, and you will have no signal that it is operating in a minefield of ambiguous cases it has never been taught to recognize.

The question worth sitting with: what would a disagreement-aware dataset look like? Not just labels, but a flag for items where N annotators produced M distinct labels. Not an error — a feature of the data that you are choosing not to model.

I do not have a clean answer for how to implement this at scale. But I keep finding that the teams who think carefully about disagreement patterns end up with better category definitions than the teams who just move the disagreement out of sight.
